title: Random fields and dependent fluid statistics

items.title: Finite-second-moment random velocity sensor law
items.design_state: authored definition with local well-definedness result
items.statement:
Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$ be a finite measure space with $0<\lambda(D)<\infty$, interpreted as a spatial region with volume measure $\lambda$. Let $H:=L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^d)$ consist of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of measurable vector fields $v$ with $\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x)<\infty$, where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm. Give $H$ the norm $\|v\|_H:=(\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x))^{1/2}$ and its norm topology; this is the finite direct sum of the scalar $L^2$ norms. Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the norm-open subsets of $H$. A finite-second-moment random velocity law is a probability measure $\mu$ on $(H,\mathcal B(H))$ such that
$$\int_H \|v\|_H^2\,d\mu(v)<\infty.$$
For a sensor weight $\psi\in H$, define the ideal linear sensor and its centered observable by
$$S_\psi(v):=\int_D v(x)\cdot\psi(x)\,d\lambda(x),\qquad
f_\psi(v):=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi(w)\,d\mu(w).$$
The sensor reads a weighted spatial average; it does not represent a point evaluation. When $v$ is assigned SI velocity units of metres per second and $\lambda$ is volume in $\mathrm m^d$, assigning $\psi$ units $\mathrm m^{-d}$ makes $S_\psi(v)$ a velocity. Other weight units multiply the sensor units by the corresponding factor. The centered observable is dimensionally the same as the sensor reading.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis, Section 11.6
Terence Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory
references.locator: Section 1.7, product-measure setup and Tonelli–Fubini context, PDF pp. 199–206.

references.title: Caroline Terquem, Fluids
references.locator: Sections 1.1.2 and 6.3.1, PDF pp. 7 and 117–120; terminology only.

items.title: The L2 velocity sensor is well-defined
items.statement:
Let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$, $H$, and the finite-second-moment probability law $\mu$ be as in the Definition. For every $\psi\in H$, the integral defining $S_\psi(v)$ is finite and independent of the representatives of $v$ and $\psi$. The map $S_\psi:H\to\mathbb R$ is linear and continuous, with
$$|S_\psi(v)|\le \|v\|_H\|\psi\|_H.$$
Its centered observable $f_\psi(v)=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi\,d\mu$ is Borel measurable and belongs to $L^2(\mu)$.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis, Section 11.6
Terence Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory
references.locator: Section 1.7, Theorem 1.7.21 and proof, printed pp. 204–206.

items.title: Quadratic velocity tensors are Bochner integrable
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$ and $H=L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^d)$ be as in the Definition, and let $K:=L^1(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ use the Frobenius norm on matrices. For $v,w\in H$, the pointwise tensor $(v\otimes w)_{ij}(x):=v_i(x)w_j(x)$ defines an element of $K$, independent of the representatives, and
$$\|v\otimes w\|_K\le \|v\|_H\|w\|_H.$$
For any probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ and strongly measurable $U:\Omega\to H$ with $\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2<\infty$, both $U$ and $U\otimes U$ are strongly measurable Bochner-integrable maps into $H$ and $K$, respectively, and
$$\mathbb E\|U\otimes U\|_K=\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2<\infty.$$

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis, Section 11.6
Terence Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory

items.axiom_use: Countable Choice is used only through Riesz-Fischer completeness of scalar L1 and L2, making the finite-component spaces H and K Banach for Bochner integration; no full AC or DC is used.

items.title: Expected weak Reynolds decomposition for a random velocity field
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$, $d$, and $H=L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^d)$ be as in the Definition. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $U:\Omega\to H$ be strongly measurable with $\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2<\infty$. Assume a representative $\widetilde U:\Omega\times D\to\mathbb R^d$ of its sections is measurable with respect to the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal D$. The Bochner mean
$$\bar u:=\int_\Omega U(\omega)\,d\mathbb P(\omega)\in H$$
is well-defined. For $\lambda$-almost every $x$, define
$$R(x):=\mathbb E\!\left[(\widetilde U(\omega,x)-\bar u(x))\otimes(\widetilde U(\omega,x)-\bar u(x))\right],$$
where any measurable representative of $\bar u$ may be used. Then $R$ determines an element of $L^1(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$, and for every measurable tensor field $\Phi:D\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ with $\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in D}|\Phi(x)|_F<\infty$,
$$\mathbb E\!\left[\int_D(\widetilde U\otimes\widetilde U):\Phi\,d\lambda\right]
=\int_D(\bar u\otimes\bar u+R):\Phi\,d\lambda.$$
For vectors $a,b\in\mathbb R^d$, $(a\otimes b)_{ij}:=a_i b_j$. Here $A:B:=\sum_{i,j=1}^d A_{ij}B_{ij}$ and $|\cdot|_F$ is the Frobenius norm. If $U$ is assigned SI velocity units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, then $\bar u$ has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $R$ has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$; the test field's units are chosen so both pairings have the same units. Here “weak” means tested against an essentially bounded tensor field. $R$ is the positive covariance tensor; no density factor, stress sign convention, incompressibility, Navier–Stokes equation, time-stationarity, or turbulence closure is assumed.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis, Section 11.6
Terence Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory
references.locator: Section 1.7, Theorems 1.7.15 and 1.7.21 with proofs, PDF pp. 200–206.

references.title: Caroline Terquem, Fluids
references.locator: Section 6.3.1, PDF pp. 117–120; Reynolds terminology only.

items.axiom_use: Countable Choice is explicitly assumed through Riesz-Fischer completeness for the finite-component L2 and L1 spaces needed for Bochner integration; no full AC or DC is used.

items.title: Long-run central limit theorem for a dependent velocity sensor
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ and the centered sensor observable $f_\psi:H\to\mathbb R$ be as in the Definition. Let $\mathcal B(H)$ be countably generated, let $P$ be a probability kernel on $(H,\mathcal B(H))$ with invariant probability $\mu$, and let $(V_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous $P$-chain whose canonical left shift preserves its path law and whose shift-invariant measurable events have probability zero or one. Assume $P$ is $\phi$-irreducible, aperiodic, and Harris recurrent for a nonzero sigma-finite measure $\phi$. Here $\phi$-irreducibility means each $\phi$-positive measurable set is reached with positive probability after some finite positive number of steps from every state; Harris recurrence means each such set is hit almost surely from every starting state; aperiodicity means there is no integer $q\ge2$ and pairwise disjoint measurable sets $H_1,\ldots,H_q$ with $\mu(H_1)>0$ and $P(v,H_{i+1})=1$ for every $v\in H_i$ and $1\le i<q$, and $P(v,H_1)=1$ for every $v\in H_q$. Invariant means $\mu P=\mu$.

For $k\ge0$, put $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(f_\psi(V_0),f_\psi(V_k))$. Suppose at least one of the following six regimes holds:

1. For some $m>1$ there is a measurable $M\ge0$ with $\int_H M\,d\mu<\infty$ and $\|P^n(v,\cdot)-\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(v)n^{-m}$ for every $v$ and $n\ge1; $f_\psi$ is essentially bounded under $\mu$.
2. For some $m>0$ there is a measurable $M\ge0$ with $\int_H M\,d\mu<\infty$ and $\|P^n(v,\cdot)-\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(v)n^{-m}$ for every $v$ and $n\ge1; for some $\delta>0$, $f_\psi\in L^{2+\delta}(\mu)$ and $m\delta>2+\delta$.
3. $P$ is geometrically ergodic, meaning $\|P^n(v,\cdot)-\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(v)r^n$ for a finite measurable $M$ and some $0<r<1$, and $f_\psi\in L^{2+\delta}(\mu)$ for some $\delta>0$.
4. $P$ is geometrically ergodic in the same total-variation sense and $\int_H f_\psi^2\log^+|f_\psi|\,d\mu<\infty$, with $0\log^+0:=0$.
5. $P$ is geometrically ergodic in the same total-variation sense, is reversible in the symmetric-flow sense $\mu(dv)P(v,dw)=\mu(dw)P(w,dv)$, and $f_\psi\in L^2(\mu)$.
6. $P$ is uniformly ergodic, meaning the geometric total-variation bound holds with $M$ bounded on $H$, and $f_\psi\in L^2(\mu)$.

Then $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$ and
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f_\psi(V_k)\ \Rightarrow\ N(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{LR}}^2(f_\psi)),$$
where $\sigma_{\mathrm{LR}}^2(f_\psi):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k$ is the covariance long-run variance. Here $\|\alpha-\beta\|_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal B(H)}|\alpha(A)-\beta(A)|$, and $f\in L^p(\mu)$ for finite $p$ means $\int_H|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty$. Also set $\log^+t:=\max(0,\log t)$ for $t>0$ and $0\log^+0:=0$. The zero-variance case is included. This is an asymptotic model deduction; it does not make finite samples normally distributed or establish a physical sensor's stationarity, Markov property, or mixing assumptions. A central limit theorem alone is not a consistency result for an estimated Monte Carlo standard error.

references.title: Galin L. Jones, On the Markov Chain Central Limit Theorem, arXiv:math/0409112v2
references.locator: Section 4.1, Theorem 9 and Corollaries 1–5, PDF pp. 9–12.

references.title: Charles J. Geyer, Markov Chain Monte Carlo Lecture Notes

items.axiom_use: AC is an explicit hypothesis, as in the MCMC CLT supplier; no stronger choice principle is used.

title: Random fields and dependent fluid statistics — Examples

items.title: A Gaussian AR(1) sensor and its long-run variance
items.statement:
Let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$, $d$, and $H$ be as in the Definition, with $\lambda(D)>0$. Let $e_1$ be the first standard basis vector in $\mathbb R^d$ and set $\psi:=e_1/\lambda(D)$. For each $x\in\mathbb R$, the spatially uniform field $V_x(y):=x e_1$ belongs to $H$ and has sensor reading $S_\psi(V_x)=x$.

Assume AC. Let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a centered, strictly stationary, jointly Gaussian time-homogeneous Markov chain on $\mathbb R$ with invariant probability $\nu=\mathcal L(X_0)$ and recursion
$$X_{n+1}=\rho X_n+\epsilon_{n+1},\qquad |\rho|<1,\quad \eta>0.$$
Assume $(\epsilon_{n})_{n\ge1}$ is an independent sequence with common law $N(0,\eta^2)$, independent of $X_0$; then the transition kernel is $P(x,\cdot)=N(\rho x,\eta^2)$. Here $N(m,v)$, for $v>0$, is the normal law with density $(2\pi v)^{-1/2}\exp(-(x-m)^2/(2v))$. “Jointly Gaussian” means every finite real linear combination of chain coordinates is normally distributed; “strictly stationary” means every finite-dimensional law is unchanged by nonnegative integer time shifts. The associated velocity-field sensor output is $Y_n:=S_\psi(V_{X_n})=X_n$. If $X_n$ has velocity units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, then $\epsilon_n$ has the same units, $\rho$ is dimensionless, and the long-run variance has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. This is a mathematical model example, not a reported fluid measurement.

For $k\ge0$, its covariance is
$$\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)=\frac{\eta^2\rho^k}{1-\rho^2}.$$
The covariance series is absolutely summable, and the centered sensor sum satisfies
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}Y_j\Rightarrow N\!\left(0,\frac{\eta^2}{(1-\rho)^2}\right).$$
Consequently its covariance long-run variance is $\sigma_{\mathrm{LR}}^2=\eta^2/(1-\rho)^2$.

references.title: Charles J. Geyer, Markov Chain Monte Carlo Lecture Notes
references.locator: Sections 4.8.1–4.9, printed pp. 132–135; the AR(1) covariance and Gaussian limit are derived locally.

references.title: Galin L. Jones, On the Markov Chain Central Limit Theorem, arXiv:math/0409112v2
references.locator: Section 4.1, Theorem 9 and Corollaries 1–5, PDF pp. 9–12; general MCMC CLT context only, with the AR(1) calculation derived locally.

items.axiom_use: AC is stated as required by the Markov-chain definition and long-run-variance supplier; no stronger choice principle is used.
